title: How to grow okra
seoTitle: How to Grow Okra: A Guide for Hot Summers
description: Grow okra in full sun and warm soil, thin plants to a foot apart, water deeply and pick pods every day or two. Tips from a North Texas okra garden.
summary: Plant okra seeds in full sun once the soil is warm, thin the plants to about a foot apart, water deeply, and pick the pods every day or two once they start. It loves heat and is one of the easiest vegetables to grow in a hot summer.

socialImage.alt: How to grow okra card with a photo of a yellow okra flower on a tall okra plant.

intro: Okra was Olivia's favorite thing to grow, and it's a good first crop for anyone. It thrives in the heat that wilts most of the garden, shrugs off dry spells, and keeps producing pods all summer.
Don't have seeds yet? Start with [free okra seeds](/okra/free-okra-seeds) from Olivia's garden.

items: Plant once the soil is at least 65°F
Seeds 1 inch deep, plants at least 1 foot apart, and we give ours 3 to 4 feet
First flowers about 2 months after planting
Pick pods at 3 to 4 inches, every day or two

blocks.text: Plant in spring 2 to 3 weeks after your last frost, once the soil is at least 65°F a few inches down. Okra seed rots in cold, wet ground, so waiting a week or two is better than planting early. See [when to plant okra](/okra/when-to-plant-okra) to find your hardiness zone and a rough planting window.

Okra needs [full sun and fertile, well-drained soil](https://agrilifeextension.tamu.edu/library/gardening/okra/) for a good crop. It grows in most soils, but does best in sandy loam with plenty of organic matter. Work the bed 8 to 10 inches deep and mix in compost before planting.

If you can, get a soil test through your county Extension office. Clemson Extension recommends a [soil pH between 5.8 and 6.5](https://hgic.clemson.edu/factsheet/how-to-grow-okra-in-south-carolina-including-planting-dates-watering-fertilizing-ratooning-pest-management-and-harvesting-tips-for-healthy-pod-production/) for okra.

items: Sow seeds straight into the garden [about 1 inch deep and 2 inches apart](https://agrilifeextension.tamu.edu/library/gardening/okra/), in rows at least 3 feet apart. Okra doesn't like being transplanted.
Some gardeners soak seeds in water overnight to help them sprout, though it won't save seed planted in cold soil. We plant ours straight from the packet without soaking or nicking them.
Keep the soil moist until the seedlings come up.
When the plants are 3 to 4 inches tall, thin them so they stand at least 1 foot apart. Ours grow so big that we space them 3 to 4 feet apart.

blocks.alt: A young okra plant in a raised garden bed with its first green pod forming at the top of the stem, next to a drip irrigation line.
blocks.caption: A young plant in Olivia's garden with its first pod.

blocks.text: Okra handles dry weather better than most vegetables, but [watering every 7 to 10 days](https://agrilifeextension.tamu.edu/library/gardening/okra/) gives a bigger harvest. Sandy soil needs water more often than clay. Water deeply enough to wet the soil about 6 inches down, since light sprinkles keep roots shallow.

Water in the morning so the leaves dry before dark, or use drip irrigation to keep the leaves dry. Steady moisture matters most [once pods start to form](https://hgic.clemson.edu/factsheet/how-to-grow-okra-in-south-carolina-including-planting-dates-watering-fertilizing-ratooning-pest-management-and-harvesting-tips-for-healthy-pod-production/). A 2 to 3 inch layer of mulch holds moisture in and keeps weeds down through the hottest part of summer.

blocks.title: From Olivia's garden
blocks.text: In McKinney summers, we run our drip line for 15 minutes every other day.

Go easy on nitrogen early. Clemson Extension notes that [too much nitrogen early in the season](https://hgic.clemson.edu/factsheet/how-to-grow-okra-in-south-carolina-including-planting-dates-watering-fertilizing-ratooning-pest-management-and-harvesting-tips-for-healthy-pod-production/) gives you a big leafy plant with few pods. We mix compost into the bed at the start of the season, before planting. If you add fertilizer, wait to feed again until the plants start producing.

Texas A&M AgriLife suggests [1 cup of garden fertilizer for every 10 feet of row](https://agrilifeextension.tamu.edu/library/gardening/okra/) after the first harvest, scattered beside the plants, mixed in lightly and watered in.

Give okra more room than you think. In our McKinney garden, Clemson Spineless plants grow over 6 feet tall and keep producing pods all season, so we plant once a year. Plan for plants that will tower over the rest of the bed and shade whatever grows on their north side. We use that shade for companion plants that do well in partial shade, like marigolds and borage.

blocks.alt: A backyard garden in late summer with bushy okra plants, tall sunflowers and corn growing below a string trellis, next to a wooden fence.
blocks.caption: Okra plants filling out the garden in late summer.

sections.title: When you'll get your first pods

blocks.text: Okra plants [flower about 2 months after planting](https://agrilifeextension.tamu.edu/library/gardening/okra/), and the pods are ready to pick 3 or 4 days after each flower opens. Pick pods at 3 to 4 inches long, every day or two. Pods left too long turn tough and stringy, and the plant slows down. By late summer we pick every day, because the pods grow fast and get too big if you skip one.

Picked often and kept watered, okra can keep producing [for up to 12 weeks](https://hgic.clemson.edu/factsheet/how-to-grow-okra-in-south-carolina-including-planting-dates-watering-fertilizing-ratooning-pest-management-and-harvesting-tips-for-healthy-pod-production/). At the end of the season, leave a few pods to dry on the plant and [save the seeds](/okra/saving-okra-seeds) for next year.

blocks.alt: A tall okra plant late in the season, covered in dried brown pods left for seed, with a few green pods still growing at the top.
blocks.caption: Late in the season, pods left on the plant dry for seed while new ones keep coming.

items: Aphids on the undersides of leaves, often with ants tending them. Clemson Extension notes that [limiting nitrogen helps](https://hgic.clemson.edu/factsheet/how-to-grow-okra-in-south-carolina-including-planting-dates-watering-fertilizing-ratooning-pest-management-and-harvesting-tips-for-healthy-pod-production/) keep them in check.
Stink bugs and leaf-footed bugs, which leave pods twisted and misshapen.
Small pods that rot after the flower drops. Full sun, good air movement and proper spacing help.
Seedlings that die soon after coming up, usually from planting into cold, wet soil.

blocks.title: From Olivia's garden
blocks.text: We sometimes get aphids, but our plants grow so vigorously that we've never lost one to them, and we don't treat. The plant wins.

faq.question: Does okra need full sun?
faq.answer: Yes. Okra needs full sun for a good harvest. In shade it grows slowly and gives few pods.

faq.question: How far apart should you plant okra?
faq.answer: Space plants at least 1 foot apart in rows 3 feet apart. In our garden the plants grow over 6 feet tall, so we give each one 3 to 4 feet.

faq.question: Why are my okra flowers falling off?
faq.answer: That's usually normal. Okra flowers are a soft, bright yellow, and each one lasts only 1 to 2 days before it drops and the pod starts to grow. If small pods are rotting after the flower falls, give the plants more sun, space and air movement.

faq.question: Can you grow okra in a pot?
faq.answer: Yes. We haven't grown okra in a container ourselves, but we've seen it grow very well in one. Container plants may be slower to start producing pods than okra in the ground.

faq.question: How long does okra take to grow?
faq.answer: Most okra flowers about 2 months after planting, and the first pods are ready a few days later.
